title: In Nepal, 6,365 refugees from Bhutan remain without legal status — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: In Nepal, 6,365 refugees from Bhutan remain without legal status — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In eastern Nepal, 6,365 refugees from Bhutan living in the Jhapa and Morang districts have been waiting for legal recognition for more than three decades. Without documents recognized by the authorities, they cannot officially work, open bank accounts, register businesses, obtain higher education or receive professional licenses, the Kathmandu Post reports.

Restrictions due to the lack of documents

The community's situation is described in a report by Peace Initiative Bhutan, prepared after visits to Beldangi in Jhapa district and Pathari in Morang district. Representatives of the organization spoke with more than 500 refugees and other stakeholders.

According to Kumar Gurung, Peace Initiative Bhutan's representative in the United States, the camps where the refugees lived have effectively turned into settlements. Their residents pay for water, electricity and waste disposal, but have no access to employment, business or professional opportunities. They also face difficulties obtaining medical care and travelling internationally.

The report states that many people depend on financial support from relatives, informal charitable assistance and donations. This limits their ability to achieve economic self-sufficiency.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Repatriation and residence in Nepal

Nepal began accepting Nepali-speaking refugees from Bhutan in the early 1990s. Bilateral attempts at a settlement did not yield results, and a third-country resettlement programme began in 2007. By 2016–2017, more than 100,000 refugees had moved, including to the United States, Australia and Norway. Those who were unable or unwilling to leave remained without a final decision on their status.

Those who remain include elderly people, single women, people with disabilities, families living in poverty, as well as children and young people born and raised in Nepal. Community representatives emphasize that for the younger generation, the opportunity to live legally in the country where they grew up is becoming increasingly important.

The report calls for refugees to be urgently issued identity cards or equivalent documents that would give them access to work, banking services, education, healthcare, birth registration and professional activity. For long-term residents of Nepal, including those born in the country, it proposes creating a transparent legal mechanism for obtaining permanent residence and, under appropriate conditions, citizenship.

title: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News - Khabarhub
description: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Economic Digest presents a brief yet comprehensive roundup of major business developments in Nepal, delivered in clear and accessible summaries.

Nepal’s economic landscape presents a mixed picture, with declining stock market activity contrasting with rising precious metal prices and continued growth in business registrations. NEPSE’s 12.95-point decline and sharp fall in turnover to Rs 4.72 billion indicate weakening investor confidence and subdued market participation. Meanwhile, surging gold and silver prices reflect growing demand for traditional safe-haven assets and heightened market uncertainty.

On the development front, infrastructure investment and public spending remain central government priorities. Irrigation projects recorded encouraging first-quarter progress, while tenders worth Rs 17.15 billion for 92 drinking water projects signal renewed efforts to expand essential services. However, the need to extend the Kathmandu-Terai Fast Track deadline highlights persistent project implementation challenges.

The government’s plan to amend 59 laws and attract alternative financing reflects recognition that regulatory barriers and declining access to concessional loans could constrain infrastructure development. Nepal-US trade discussions and growing company registrations offer opportunities to strengthen private investment and economic diversification.

Meanwhile, agricultural initiatives, recovering egg production and increased mountaineering royalties demonstrate potential in productive sectors. However, persistent LPG shortages and unresolved land ownership issues expose weaknesses in market distribution and governance.

Overall, Nepal needs to translate policy reforms, rising investment interest and development spending into efficient implementation, employment generation and sustainable economic growth.

NEPSE sheds 12.95 points as turnover drops to Rs 4.72 billion

The Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) index declined by 12.95 points to close at 2,652.58 on Thursday, while daily turnover dropped to Rs 4.72 billion from Rs 7.43 billion recorded on Wednesday. Of the 13 trading subgroups, only microfinance registered a marginal gain, while the remaining 12 ended in negative territory. Share prices of 211 companies declined, while 56 advanced and 12 remained unchanged. None of the advancing stocks recorded gains exceeding 3 percent. The 10.25 percent KBL Debenture-2026 posted the steepest loss, falling 5.09 percent. Chir Khwa Hydropower followed with a decline of around 4.5 percent. Ankhu Khola Hydropower Company led the turnover chart, with shares worth Rs 181.9 million traded. Nepal Reinsurance Company ranked second, recording transactions worth more than Rs 145 million.

Gold price jumps Rs 13,300 per tola, silver rises Rs 265

Gold and silver prices recorded sharp increases in the domestic market on Thursday, with gold rising by Rs 13,300 and silver by Rs 265 per tola. According to the Federation of Nepal Gold and Silver Dealers’ Association, the price of hallmark gold has been fixed at Rs 288,900 per tola, while silver is being traded at Rs 3,920 per tola. On Wednesday, hallmark gold was priced at Rs 275,600 per tola and silver at Rs 3,655. One tola is equivalent to approximately 11.66 grams.

NRB begins Tihar sale of gold coins and silver medallions

The Mint Division of Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) began selling gold asarfis and silver medallions to the public on Thursday as part of its annual Tihar promotion. The sale will continue until Friday, the final day of the festive campaign. According to the NRB’s Currency Management Department, a 2.5-gram gold coin is priced at Rs 65,400, while a 10-gram silver medallion costs Rs 3,800. The central bank has introduced the seasonal sale to enable people to purchase gold and silver items for the festival, during which precious metals are traditionally bought and exchanged as gifts.

Irrigation projects spend Rs 2.39 billion in first quarter

Irrigation projects operating under the Department of Water Resources and Irrigation spent Rs 2.39 billion during the first quarter of fiscal year 2026/27, with capital expenditure, mainly on construction activities, accounting for 88 percent of the total. Department Director General Dinesh Rajauria said the Mahakali Irrigation Project in Kanchanpur achieved 97.2 percent of its quarterly physical progress target, spending Rs 437 million, more than two and a half times its allocated quarterly budget. The Babai, Sikta and Rani Jamara Kulariya irrigation projects achieved 81.8 percent, 80.2 percent and 71 percent of their respective physical targets. Together, the four major projects, including Mahakali, spent Rs 1.39 billion, accounting for 58 percent of the department’s total expenditure. Meanwhile, the Praganna-Badkapath Project in Dang recorded 88.2 percent physical progress, while the Deep Tubewell Irrigation Project and the Irrigation Institutional Development Program achieved their full quarterly targets.

Govt extends company compliance deadline, registrations continue to rise

The government has extended the deadline for companies to update their records and qualify for fines and penalties exemptions by two months, moving it from mid-November to mid-January. The extension is intended to provide companies with additional time to complete their compliance requirements and avoid penalties related to fiscal year 2025/26. The Registrar of the Office of Company Registrar has emphasized the need for companies to comply with the Companies Act, 2006. Company registrations have continued to increase, rising from 20,736 in fiscal year 2024/25 to 26,291 in fiscal year 2025/26. A further 10,480 companies had been registered by October of the current fiscal year, partly attributed to returning Nepali nationals investing in the domestic economy. The total number of registered companies has reached 388,690, while 14,970 companies have been deregistered. The Office of Company Registrar is responsible for overseeing company registration, regulatory compliance and liquidation procedures.

PM’s relief funds receive Rs 18.37 billion, including $31.42 million in foreign currency

Contributions to the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund and the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund have continued following the floods in Rasuwa and along the Bhote Koshi River, taking their combined deposits to Rs 18.37 billion as of 9 am on Thursday. According to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers, Rs 13.62 billion has been deposited in nine accounts maintained at different commercial banks. The funds also hold USD 31.42 million in foreign currency accounts at Himalayan Bank and Laxmi Sunrise Bank.

Three ministers outline legal reforms and preparations for Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026

Law Minister Sobita Gautam, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal have outlined preparations for the upcoming Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026, highlighting plans to amend 59 laws covering 494 provisions to improve the investment climate. Speaking on Thursday, Gautam said more than 54 bills had already advanced through the Cabinet as part of the government’s legal reform agenda. Finance Minister Wagle said the summit would focus on presenting economic and legal reforms already implemented rather than simply announcing investment commitments. He also stressed the importance of involving the private sector in major infrastructure development projects. Infrastructure Development Minister Lamsal said the proposed legislative changes would address issues related to investment, taxation and land management. He also highlighted plans to promote the use of domestic raw materials in both public and private sector projects to reduce implementation delays and support local industries.

Foreign Ministry discusses Nepal-US trade and investment promotion

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs organized an interactive discussion on Wednesday focusing on the promotion of Nepal-US trade and investment, as well as exchanges of visits between the private sectors of the two countries. Addressing the programme, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal stressed the importance of promoting Nepal as an emerging economy and an attractive destination for foreign investment. He called for coordinated efforts to increase exports, attract more foreign tourists and support economic growth while ensuring good governance. During the programme, the American Chamber of Commerce in Nepal and the Nepal-USA Chamber of Commerce and Industry (NUSACCI) presented papers highlighting investment opportunities, trade prospects and challenges in Nepal-US economic relations. Representatives from major business organizations, including the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FNCCI), Confederation of Nepalese Industries (CNI), Nepal Chamber of Commerce, Federation of Export Entrepreneurs Nepal (FEEN) and Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), also participated. Representatives of various startups were among those attending the discussion.

Govt invites bids for 92 drinking water projects worth Rs 17.15 billion

The government has invited tenders for 92 drinking water projects worth a combined Rs 17.15 billion during the first three months of fiscal year 2026/27. The projects aim to extend safe drinking water services to more than 1.3 million people across various districts within the next 30 months. According to information released by the Secretariat of the Ministry of Infrastructure Development, the tenders were published through the Department of Water Supply and Sewerage Management. The government plans to initiate procurement processes for drinking water projects worth up to Rs 44 billion during the current fiscal year. No contracts for such projects were awarded in the previous fiscal year due to the absence of agreements concerning water sources. The government has set a target of ensuring access to safe drinking water for all citizens at their doorsteps by fiscal year 2030/31.

Defence Ministry spends 26.87 percent of annual budget in first quarter

The Ministry of Defence has reported progress in its development projects, spending 26.87 percent of its total annual budget by Wednesday, November 4, during the first quarter of fiscal year 2026/27. According to the ministry, recurrent expenditure reached 104.09 percent of the first-quarter target against an annual allocation of Rs 60.3 billion. Capital expenditure stood at 43.24 percent of its first-quarter target against an annual allocation of Rs 6.28 billion. The Kathmandu-Terai/Madhesh Fast Track, a national pride project, recorded 50.54 percent overall physical progress, while its financial progress reached 52 percent. The project’s completion deadline has been extended to mid-March 2030 to address initial challenges related to the alignment of the road section in Kathmandu.

Nepal needs alternative financing as concessional loans become limited: Wagle

Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle has said Nepal must explore alternative financing options for large infrastructure projects as access to highly concessional loans from the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) is expected to become increasingly limited. Speaking at a press conference on the Nepal Infrastructure Summit 2026 on Thursday, Wagle said Nepal had traditionally relied on highly concessional financing from the two multilateral development institutions, although the availability of such loans had increasingly become a matter of debate. He noted that loans offering repayment periods of 35 to 40 years and interest rates of around 1 to 1.5 percent in US dollars had provided an important financing option for major infrastructure projects. However, as access to such funding becomes more constrained, Nepal needs to identify and pursue alternative sources of investment, he said. Wagle also said the upcoming infrastructure summit would focus on showcasing reforms already introduced by the government rather than making fresh promises about future initiatives. He added that the government was pursuing economic and legal reforms, including amendments to 59 laws, compared with 65 laws enacted over the preceding three and a half years.

Gandaki signs Rs 14.3 million agreement with Paiyun for agricultural project

The Gandaki Province government and Paiyun Rural Municipality in Parbat district signed an agreement on Wednesday, November 4, to implement a women-led high-tech tunnel farming and smart agricultural market management project. The initiative, being implemented under the Chief Minister Innovation Partnership Program, has an estimated total cost of Rs 14.3 million. Under the cost-sharing arrangement, the Gandaki Province government will contribute Rs 10.6 million, while Paiyun Rural Municipality will provide the remaining Rs 3.7 million. The project aims to expand off-season vegetable production through the construction of high-tech agricultural tunnels, establishment of collection centres and introduction of web- and mobile-based software for market management. It will also focus on creating commercial opportunities for local women farmers and strengthening agricultural marketing systems in the area.

Foreign climbers generate Rs 323.7 million in royalties during autumn season

Foreign mountaineering expeditions generated more than USD 2.1 million, equivalent to Rs 323.7 million, in royalty revenue for Nepal during the 2026 autumn climbing season as of October 29. According to the Department of Tourism, 1,493 climbers, including 1,137 men and 356 women, from 171 international expedition teams representing 76 countries obtained climbing permits. Mount Manaslu remained the most popular destination, attracting 500 climbers, including 373 men and 127 women, across 43 expedition teams. The mountain generated more than USD 1.4 million, equivalent to Rs 225.8 million, in royalties. Mount Ama Dablam was another major attraction, generating USD 404,000, or approximately Rs 61.6 million, in royalties from 412 permitted climbers.

FAO and NSO launch joint study on youth participation in agriculture

The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Nepal and the National Statistics Office (NSO) have launched a joint initiative to assess young people’s participation in the country’s agriculture and agrifood sectors. The two institutions will jointly prepare a statistical report titled Status of Youth Engagement in Nepal’s Agriculture and Agrifood Systems. An inception meeting was held to initiate the process of consolidating national data on youth participation in the sector. The study aims to provide a comprehensive picture of young people’s involvement, opportunities and challenges across agriculture and agrifood systems. According to the initiative, its findings will provide an evidence base for formulating policies, programmes and investments that better address the needs and participation of young people. The initiative is also expected to support the development of more inclusive and sustainable agrifood systems in Nepal. This marks the first joint statistical assessment of youth engagement in the sector undertaken by FAO Nepal and the NSO.

Janak-Sarakar campaign seeks improvements in Janakpurdham railway services

The Janak-Sarakar Campaign has submitted a memorandum to Nepal Railway Company, calling for improved management and passenger-friendly facilities across the Janakpurdham railway network. The campaign delegation highlighted Janakpurdham’s cultural, religious and historical importance and urged the railway authorities to ensure better safety, cleanliness and passenger convenience. The memorandum includes demands for regular maintenance of platforms, proper operation of electrical equipment, clean public toilets and reliable drinking water facilities. It has also called for developing unused railway land into public parks and organized marketplaces. Similarly, the campaign has urged authorities to introduce safety measures at railway crossings to prevent accidents and bring freight transportation services into operation to promote regional trade. The delegation stressed the need to improve railway services since their resumption on April 2, 2022.

Chhimek Laghubitta and Api Power announce proposed dividends

Two companies listed on the Nepal Stock Exchange (NEPSE) have announced proposed dividend distributions to shareholders for the previous fiscal year. Chhimek Laghubitta Bittiya Sanstha Limited has proposed a total dividend of 25 percent, comprising 11.96 percent bonus shares and 13.03 percent cash dividends. The proposed distribution is subject to approval from Nepal Rastra Bank and endorsement at the company’s upcoming annual general meeting. Similarly, Api Power Company has proposed a total dividend of 5.0263 percent, consisting of 5 percent bonus shares and 0.263 percent cash dividends to cover applicable taxes. The proposed dividend distribution by Api Power is subject to approval from the Electricity Regulatory Commission and endorsement by the company’s annual general meeting.

Bhaktapur households struggle with persistent LP gas shortages

Residents across Bhaktapur district continue to face difficulties obtaining liquefied petroleum (LP) gas cylinders despite official claims that market supplies have returned to normal. Although the District Administration Office had announced that distribution had stabilized following Dashain, consumers say they are still struggling to obtain filled cylinders from retailers and distributors. Several households have reportedly been waiting for up to three months to exchange their empty cylinders, forcing some to approach multiple retailers or seek alternative cooking fuels. Before major festivals, the administration had published distribution schedules on social media to facilitate supplies. However, the absence of clear delivery schedules and transparent cylinder exchange arrangements among different gas companies has further complicated the situation. The continuing shortage has caused growing frustration among consumers, who have called for more effective monitoring and reliable distribution arrangements.

Egg production in Dang recovers to over 2,500 cartons daily

Daily egg production in Dang district has recovered to more than 2,500 cartons following efforts by poultry farmers to stabilize the market and improve the prices they receive. Each carton contains 210 eggs. Production had previously fallen from between 5,000 and 6,000 cartons to around 1,000 cartons a day due to weak demand and inadequate market prices. According to the Nepal Layers Poultry Farmers Association, Dang, improved coordination among more than 150 affiliated farmers, who collectively operate around 900,000 layer chickens, has helped reduce financial losses. Association Secretary Rabindra Bikram KC said more than 45 new entrepreneurs enter the poultry business in the district every year. Around 20 percent of the daily production, equivalent to approximately 500 cartons, is consumed locally, while the remaining 80 percent is supplied to outside markets. A depot established in Tulsipur in collaboration with Nepal Egg Trading has introduced a centralized sales system. The price of an individual egg has been fixed at Rs 19.12. Association Central President Binod Pokharel said the system was introduced to prevent farmers from being forced to sell eggs below production costs.

Arun-III targets commercial power generation by February 2028

The 900-megawatt Arun-III Hydroelectric Project is targeting commercial electricity generation by February 2028 (Falgun 2084 BS), as efforts continue to resolve longstanding implementation challenges. The Investment Board Nepal advanced administrative procedures to address the project’s outstanding issues during its 68th board meeting held on October 9. Being constructed in Sankhuwasabha by SJVN Arun-III Power Development Company, the project has achieved 77.5 percent physical progress in its power generation facilities. Meanwhile, construction of the 253-kilometre, 400 kV cross-border transmission line connecting the project to Sitamarhi in India has reached 60 percent completion. The project has an estimated total cost of Rs 144 billion. Under the project agreement, Nepal will receive 21.9 percent of the electricity generated free of cost, equivalent to 197 megawatts at full capacity. The agreement also provides for royalty payments to Nepal over the project’s 25-year operational period.

Land settlement commission receives over 60,000 applications in Jhapa

The Land Problem Settlement Commission in Jhapa has received applications from 60,570 families seeking land ownership certificates. According to the commission, the applicants include 2,896 landless Dalit families, 15,783 landless families and 41,851 families classified as unorganized settlers. The commission has also received 5,296 applications carried forward from the previous commission. Commission Chair and Chief District Officer said revised land revenue rates have been fixed at 12 percent for residential land and 7 percent for agricultural land. During visits to various municipalities on Monday and Tuesday, Minister for Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration Pratibha Rawal discussed priorities for distributing land ownership certificates with commission officials and chief administrative officers of local governments. Rawal reaffirmed the government’s commitment to finding a lasting solution to land-related problems in the district.

title: Nepal’s Supreme Court postpones decision on registering Karki’s petition — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal’s Supreme Court postpones decision on registering Karki’s petition — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal’s Supreme Court has postponed a decision on registering a petition by Dan Bahadur Karki, who is challenging his removal from the post of inspector general of police. Lawyer Tika Bahadur Kunwar submitted the document on his behalf on November 5, and the court administration said it needed time to review it. As The Kathmandu Post reports, Supreme Court registrar Tagindra Kattel said a decision on registration was to be made on November 6.

Claims in the petition

Karki is asking for the government’s decision to appoint him as the prime minister’s special adviser on security to be annulled and for him to be reinstated as police chief until the completion of his legally stipulated term. He also demands that newly appointed police chief Manjaya Kumar K C be temporarily barred from performing the duties of inspector general while the case is under consideration.

The petition states that the government removed Karki before the end of his term without giving him an opportunity to respond to the grounds for the decision. The petitioner believes that appointment to another post cannot be a means of circumventing the legal safeguards established for dismissing the police chief.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Appointment of a new chief

The Cabinet removed Karki from office and appointed him as the prime minister’s security adviser. Additional Inspector General Manjaya Kumar K C was appointed the new police chief and has already assumed his duties.

The petition also seeks to have K C’s appointment and related decisions declared invalid. The petitioner asks that K C justify the legality of holding the post and that Karki be allowed to remain police chief until the end of the service term set by the Nepal Police Regulations of 2014. Karki had led the police since November 2025, and his term was to last until March 2028.

If the petition is registered, a hearing may be scheduled after the Tihar holiday recess, when the court resumes work. The court may issue an interim order preserving the status quo and summon the parties, or first require them to provide explanations regarding interim measures.

title: LMC constructs public park with Swiss aid - The Rising Nepal
description: LMC constructs public park with Swiss aid  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By Binu Shrestha,Lalitpur, Nov. 6: Lalitpur Metropolitan City (LMC) has constructed a public park named 'Nhu Pukhu Avenue' alongside Nhu Pokhari in Lagankhel, with financial and technical assistance from the Swiss government. The park was inaugurated on Thursday.

The park was jointly inaugurated by LMC Mayor Chiri Babu Maharjan and the President of the National Council of Switzerland, Pierre-André Page. Named 'Nhu Pukhu Avenue', the public space is regarded as a symbol of the enduring friendship between Switzerland and Nepal.

The park was constructed with financial and technical support from the Swiss government under an agreement with LMC. According to the metropolitan city, the total construction cost of the park was Rs. 22.5 million. The park covers an area of 2 ropanis and 4 annas and is located in Ward No. 5.

Speaking at the inauguration ceremony, Mayor Chiri Babu Maharjan said the park represents the relationship between the people of Switzerland and Nepal. He said, "On the occasion of the 70th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between Nepal and Switzerland, the Swiss government proposed constructing a park, and we accepted the proposal. The place where we are standing today is the result of that initiative."

Stating that unnecessary structures had been removed to make way for the park, Mayor

Maharjan said, "You all know what this place looked like before and how it looks now." He added that the metropolitan city and its residents would take care of the park as if nurturing their own children. He also invited President Pierre-André Page and his delegation to visit Nepal again.

"Once is not enough to visit Nepal. Please come again. By then, the other ponds here will also be filled with water, and fireflies will appear at night," he said. President of the Swiss National Council, Pierre-André Page, thanked Lalitpur Metropolitan City and its residents for their warm hospitality.

Noting that Switzerland, like Nepal, is also a country with many mountains, he said the park would further strengthen the relationship between the two countries.

Expressing his desire to visit Nepal again, President Page pledged to return to see the ponds filled with water.

KATHMANDU, Nov 6: The Nepal Police have enforced the 'Special Security Plan, 2083' focusing on the major festivals of the Nepali people, including Tihar, Nepal Sambat and Chhath.

(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});

The police have made special security arrangements to maintain peace and security and check possible criminal and untoward activities during the festive time.

According to the Police Headquarters, police personnel have been deployed as needed to control theft, robbery, gambling, betting, quarrels, and other criminal activities that may occur during festivals.

Special surveillance and checks have been intensified in public transport areas, main market areas, border areas, and customs points.

Related story Special security plan for upcoming festivals implemented in Chi...

Spokesperson at the Nepal Police, Abhi Narayan Kafle, informed that fire and disaster management teams have been kept on standby round the clock considering the risk of fire and accidents from lamps, lights, and fireworks during Tihar.

He shared that local administrations have been urged to carry out the Deusi-Bhailo programmes in a regulated manner within the set time.

Similarly, special patrol teams have been deployed at borders, customs areas, and markets to control the illegal trafficking, storage, and sale of fireworks and other explosive materials.

The police have raised public awareness through local radio, newspapers, and social media, and urged the public not to be involved in light fireworks, gambling or betting, creating disturbances under alcoholic influence, and to celebrate the festivals peacefully.

Plainclothes police have been mobilized in areas where gambling and other unintended activities might occur.

Spokesperson Kafle said security arrangements have been beefed up to reduce disputes and clashes that could happen between two communities during rallies and processions organized on festive occasions.

He added that monitoring has been increased considering the possible impact on the elderly, children, and patients from activities like playing loud music with DJs and sound systems, bursting firecrackers, and doing fireworks late at night.

Special attention has been given to controlling potential activities related to domestic violence, beatings, and personal disputes.

The police have urged people to immediately inform the nearest police station, fire department, or relevant authorities in case of fire, explosion, or any other accident, and to help quickly rescue the injured and take them to the nearest health facility.

The police have also requested the general public to report to the police hotline 100 if anyone sees illegal trading, storage, or use of firecrackers and explosives.

title: Vikram Misri calls on Nepal PM , discusses bilateral ties - The Tribune

India and Nepal have agreed to step up cooperation across traditional and emerging sectors, including hydropower, connectivity, trade, digital technology and artificial intelligence, ahead of Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s forthcoming visit to India.

Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri, who concluded a two-day visit to Kathmandu on Thursday, called on Shah and conveyed greetings from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while discussing the progress of bilateral cooperation and possible outcomes of the Nepalese leader’s upcoming India visit.

A joint press release issued after Misri’s November 4-5 visit said the two sides reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening the bilateral partnership across sectors, with both countries noting growing engagement in areas ranging from development cooperation and energy to startups, digital connectivity, AI and sports.

Misri also called on Nepal’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha and Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal.

title: Nepal sets up round-the-clock centre to combat online financial scams - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal sets up round-the-clock centre to combat online financial scams  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The government is launching a round-the-clock cyber response centre on Friday to tackle the growing incidence of financial fraud linked to digital banking, mobile wallets, online payment platforms and social media.

The Integrated Anti-Cyber Scam Response Centre has been established at the new building of the Nepal Police Cyber Bureau in Samakhusi under the Guideline on the Establishment and Operation of the Integrated Anti-Cyber Scam Response Centre 2026, approved by the home ministry.

Representatives from the Nepal Police, Nepal Rastra Bank, banks and financial institutions, payment service providers, telecommunications companies and internet service providers will work together at the centre. The aim is to freeze money before scammers can withdraw or transfer it, while identifying and dismantling the networks behind the fraud.

On Thursday, Nepal Rastra Bank issued a notice asking development banks, finance companies, payment system operators and payment service providers to submit the names, mobile numbers and email addresses of their designated liaison officers.

Representatives of commercial banks, Nepal Telecom, Ncell, payment service providers Khalti and eSewa, the Internet Service Providers Association, Nepal Police and the central bank will be required to maintain a physical presence at the centre around the clock, working in three shifts.

The centre will operate under strict response deadlines designed to address a major weakness in the handling of online fraud: delays caused by conventional investigation procedures and coordination between multiple agencies, which often leave victims unable to recover their money.

Under the prescribed workflow, complaints received through a hotline, information channels, the Nagarik App, Nepal Police App, the centre’s online portal or other platforms will be entered into a case management system within ten minutes. A reference number will be generated, and the incident will be classified and prioritised according to the nature and pattern of the suspected scam within the same period.

Within ten to 30 minutes, designated officials from banks, payment service providers and payment system operators are expected to identify the beneficiary account or wallet, the timing of transactions and the trail of funds.

Between ten and 60 minutes, the centre will send simultaneous requests to the relevant bank or wallet provider to freeze the account and funds. If the money has already been transferred to other accounts, officials will follow the transaction trail and seek to freeze the funds at each subsequent destination.

The same 60-minute window will be used to initiate parallel action to deactivate mobile numbers and SIM cards used in the scam, and to block phishing domains and IP addresses through internet service providers.

Home ministry spokesperson Ananda Kafle said preparations for the centre’s operation had been completed. “The ministry has already directed the relevant agencies to bring everyone together at the Cyber Bureau so that the centre can begin operations on Friday,” Kafle said. “We are bringing the call centre and representatives of the concerned agencies under one roof because delays in coordination can mean that money has already disappeared in digital fraud cases.”

The central objective is to prevent stolen money from leaving the financial system, said Deputy Superintendent of Police Deepak Raj Awasthi, who is also spokesperson for the Cyber Bureau.

In the past, poor coordination between agencies meant that even the exchange of official letters could take months, while victims were often forced to pursue cases for up to a year, he said. “Our main goal is to have everyone working together so that funds can be frozen immediately. We want to make sure scammers do not get the chance to withdraw the money,” Awasthi said.

Initially, complaints received through the hotline will be recorded in Excel sheets or an internal system. With bank representatives physically present at the centre, authorities expect account freezes to be processed more quickly. “This is a good example of a public-private partnership,” Awasthi said. “It will also give banks and financial institutions a closer understanding of the complexities of police investigations and the difficulties faced by victims.”

The guideline sets out a broader mandate to prevent and investigate fraud involving the misuse of electronic platforms, strengthen trust in the country’s financial system and protect the public from cyber scams.

Among its objectives are establishing a single point of contact that operates 24 hours a day, creating an effective mechanism to identify and freeze bank and wallet accounts as soon as a complaint is received, and disabling the digital tools used by scammers. These include mobile numbers, SIM cards, bulk SMS services, sender IDs, phishing domains, IP addresses, malicious links and applications.

The centre’s responsibilities will range from registering, classifying and prioritising complaints to tracing the movement of stolen money and identifying the accounts or wallets that ultimately benefit from the fraud.

The guideline provides for a three-tier structure to oversee the centre, coordinate operations and provide policy direction.

At the highest level, a 12-member steering committee will be chaired by the joint secretary of the Home Ministry’s Security and Coordination Division. Its members will include representatives from the Finance Ministry, the Law Division, the Information Technology and Electronic Governance Office, the Department of Money Laundering Investigation, the Office of the Attorney General, Nepal Rastra Bank, the Cyber Bureau, the Nepal Telecommunications Authority, the Nepal Bankers’ Association and the Internet Service Providers Association. The committee’s secretariat will be based at the Home Ministry.

The second tier will be an operations coordination committee chaired by the director of Nepal Rastra Bank’s Payment Systems Department, with its secretariat at the central bank. It will oversee the effectiveness of the centre’s operations, facilitate the analysis of money trails and collection of evidence, and monitor the performance of officials deployed at the centre.

At the operational level, a team led by a Nepal Police superintendent will handle the centre’s day-to-day work around the clock.

A software system called AFRS, which is under development, is expected to automate several functions. It will send immediate cyber threat and fraud alerts to banks and financial institutions, record incoming calls and complaints, and maintain a centralised database.

A total of 114 personnel will be deployed across three shifts, according to the guideline. The Nepal Police will provide 33 personnel, including nine in each shift and six for daily operations.

The country’s 20 Class ‘A’ commercial banks will contribute 60 representatives, with 20 deployed in each shift. Nepal Telecom and Ncell will provide six representatives between them, while Nepal Rastra Bank, the Internet Service Providers Association and the Development Bankers Association Nepal will each provide three. Khalti and eSewa will each assign one representative per shift, bringing their combined total to six.

Other development banks, finance companies, payment service providers and payment system operators will not be required to station representatives at the centre. Instead, they must designate liaison officers available around the clock to coordinate with the response team from their respective offices. The central bank has asked these institutions to submit their officers’ contact details.

The private technology sector has welcomed the initiative, but cautions that setting up the centre alone will not eliminate cyber fraud.

Sajan Sharma, chief executive of City Tech and a former president of Fintech Alliance Nepal, described the centre as a positive first step towards improving information-sharing across the financial technology sector.

“Monitoring and maintaining visibility over fintech companies at the central bank level is a welcome initiative,” Sharma said. “It can make the flow of information between the central bank and other participants in the ecosystem faster and more efficient.”

title: Importance Of Crow In Tihar - The Rising Nepal
description: Importance Of Crow In Tihar  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Tihar is the second most important Hindu festival in Nepal. It starts with Kaag (crow) Tihar. Kaag Tihar is the first day of Yamapanchak. It's a five-day-long festival that lasts from Kartik Krishna Trayodashi to Kartik Shukla Dwitiya.

This festival is dedicated to Yamaraj, the Hindu god of death. This day also marks the birth anniversary of Lord Dhanvantari, the god of Ayurveda.

In Hindu mythology, crows play an important role. Crows are considered to be the messengers of Yamaraj, connecting Martyaloka (our world) with Yamaloka (the world of the dead).

On the first day of Yamapanchak, it is believed that crows come from Yamaloka to the living world. Hence, people perform Kaag Puja by offering sweets and traditional foods to crows. They believe that this will bring good fortune and luck to their family throughout the year.

Crows have significant importance from cultural perspective. We have idioms like Kaag-gaveshan (searching with dedication), Kaag-nyaya (logic) and Kaag-bali (offerings). People offer a portion of their food to crows before eating in many Hindu families.

Yamapanchak is also performed by worshipping Lord Yama and lighting an oil lamp (Yamadeepadanam). Many people buy new kitchen items on this day. It is considered lucky to buy copper and brass items but unlucky to buy iron items.





The birthday of Lord Dhanvantari is celebrated by Ayurvedic practitioners, traditional healers and those who follow Vedic medicine. He is highly respected for being the divine father of Ayurveda.

Tihar is celebrated with Lakshmi Puja followed by Govardhan Puja. The festival ends with Bhai Tika.

It is believed that, Yamuna, the sister of Yamaraj, sent a message to Yamaraj through a crow. When he arrived, she offered him colourful tika, mustard oil, a flower garland made from makhamali (globe amaranth) flowers and dubo (Bermuda grass). The day shares the strong bond between brothers and sisters.

There are many references to Kakabhushundi, an immortal sage in Hindu scriptures such as the Ramcharitmanas and Yogavasishtha. He takes the form of a crow and dedicates himself to Lord Rama. Crows are also associated with ancestor worship during Pitri Paksha. Food (especially cooked rice during Pinda Daan) is offered to crows. The birds are also associated with Shani Dev, the god of Saturn. His vahana is believed to be a crow. Offering crows black sesame seeds and other offerings is considered to help relieve bad karma, especially on Saturday.

Crows are very clever and social creatures. They can recognise human faces, remember dangers and warn other birds. They can solve problems and create tools. Their brains are very tightly packed, and they have highly developed cognitive abilities despite not having a neocortex like mammals. They are scavengers and help keep the environment clean by eating rotting matter.

The crow is more than just a religious symbol. They represent ancestors, messages from gods, cleverness, socialisation and a balanced ecosystem. Hindus celebrate Kaag Tihar to show appreciation for this incredible creature. It reminds us that we need to respect and live in harmony with nature.

(The author is a wildlife photographer. The photos used in this article are by the author.)

title: Rethinking Nepal’s Development Finance - The Rising Nepal
description: Rethinking Nepal’s Development Finance  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
The devastating floods of the Bhotekoshi, the Kali Gandaki and the Budhi Gandaki River corridors during late August to early October 2026 in the Himalayan Mountains have warned us about the vulnerability of Nepal’s development finance model. These floods, possibly triggered by climate-induced tragedies, have swept away strategic bridges and people's houses and severely damaged infrastructure. This is not the exception, as Nepal has been witnessing similar disasters over the last few years.

Together, these cyclical disasters have been warning the authorities to rethink the development and public investment model the country has been adopting for the last three or more decades. There is a fundamental ambiguity about our capacity to finance infrastructure, which was undermined in considering, informing, and managing the geographical and climatic risks to which the country is vulnerable. The fundamental infrastructures such as roads, bridges, business corridors, human settlements and hydropower projects remain vulnerable to extreme climatic floods, landslides and sudden changes in river behaviour.

Risk planning

The very preliminary assessment by the government estimates around Rs. 400 billion in asset damage and economic losses from the August Bhotekoshi disaster alone. In the meantime, the Kali Gandaki and Budhi Gandaki rivers repeatedly washed away several strategic infrastructures and means of livelihood. Here the fundamental question is not simply how quickly we can rebuild the damaged public properties but why our public investments continue to be exposed to such devastating risks in the first place.

The vital question is whether we should keep investing public resources in the same development patterns that again and again expose people, infrastructure and public finances to intolerable risks. Now the time has come that the nation needs an immediate shift in both infrastructure planning and development finance.

Over time, the country’s development priorities have been severely guided by political promises, election consciousness and the undue charm of large infrastructure projects. Often it is observed that the roads, bridges and other physical structures with very little value addition for the economy are counted as symbols of progress and political achievement. However, vulnerability assessment, antagonistic climate risks, river dynamics and long-term liabilities have not always received the attention they deserve.

It is obvious that the country needs better connectivity, reliable energy, resilient settlements and productive infrastructure, but it should be linked to employment, income and socioeconomic transformation of the community. Nepal, a country with steep slopes, fragile geological formations and unpredictable river systems, cannot rely only on conventional tools of development planning and investment modelling.

The burning issue of climate change has been complicating the planning and budgeting process as illustrated by the latest climate-induced disasters. It says how a hazard originating in a remote mountain catchment can cascade downstream, destroying infrastructure and livelihoods far beyond its point of origin. Such events warn the planner why risk-informed planning and budgeting are the most resilient strategic infrastructure networks.

Development economics

Flaws of the development model cannot be explained by technical limitations alone. It has a strong association with the political economy of public investment, procurement and natural-resource management. Economists believe that large public investments create opportunities for augmented economic activities and promote private sectors. However, it has been a common practice that the selection of strategic projects followed by the financial closure, procurement, construction and environmental regulation were often guided by political influence, resulting in conflicts of interest and rent-seeking incentives.

It was an open secret that the nexus among the political actors, public officials, regulators and business inflated project costs, compromised environmental safeguards and distorted engineering standards. Such a nexus resulted in a poorly regulated extraction of natural resources that was responsible for changing river channels, destabilising riverbanks and weakening nearby infrastructure.

In the meantime, politically exposed individuals and businesses knowingly occupy risky locations because of land market incentives and weak enforcement due to undue favours from the leadership. It would be unfair to attribute every incident to political economy, but we must acknowledge that the unchecked nexus creates risks for emergency services, public infrastructure and the wider economy.

The distorted development finance impacts far beyond the cost of reconstruction, affecting public revenue, household income, private investment and the government’s ability to finance essential services. When roads and bridges are destroyed, transport and trade are disrupted, and associated revenue declines, which in turn affects livelihoods, raises insurance claims and drags the economy into recession.

In response, public funds get diverted towards emergency relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction, creating a vicious cycle of fiscal burden. The government opted for debt financing to build infrastructure, but the misguided risk management and political-economy nexus leave these investments vulnerable to destruction, making new borrowing compulsory to restore what was lost. Meanwhile, debt-servicing obligations continue, even when the assets financed by borrowing are no longer delivering their expected economic and social returns.

Nepal cannot sustain such a vicious cycle, and the debt, which is supposed to finance productive assets, cannot repeatedly fund the replacement of infrastructure whose risks were ignored in the first place. This is creating a 'Double Shoulders' challenge for the present government, i.e. mobilise the finance for reconstruction and recovery while protecting the public budget from the recurrence of avoidable losses.

Opportunity for reforms

The present government has an opportunity to address this fundamental problem of development finance. Recovery is a pragmatic tool for rethinking development policies, institutional practices and investment modelling to avoid recurring loss and damage.

First of all, an evidence-based review of engineering codes and infrastructure standards for high-risk areas, with a flexible clause that allows such standards to be periodically updated with evolving evidence. Second, climate-induced disaster risk screening should be made mandatory for major public infrastructure investments.

Thirdly, risk-based zoning of river corridors with strong regulation is essential, especially for the areas that are exposed to exceptional flood and climate-induced hazards. In case of unavoidable risks, critical infrastructure and human settlements should be restricted or relocated with practical alternatives.

Fourthly, river-based material extraction must be governed by science-based limits rather than short-term revenue considerations. Finally, indigenous knowledge and skills should be institutionalised with proper testing and documentation in the development model.

Policy and planning reforms alone will not work unless Nepal rethinks how it mobilises and invests development finance. Tax-based budgets and debt financing are already under pressure from competing demands for infrastructure, social protection, universal health, education and unforeseen economic recovery.

It is high time for the government to implement a diversified framework for alternative development finance. However, alternative development finance must not become another route for contingent liabilities to invest in poorly appraised projects. As the conventional Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) could not work as expected, it requires rigorous value-for-money assessments and transparent disclosure of the government’s long-term financial commitments.

Investments in early-warning systems, river monitoring, hazard mapping, resilient infrastructure and planned relocation may not produce the immediate political visibility like a road or bridge, but their economic returns can be substantial when measured against avoided losses.

Development financing should be evaluated by whether such investments help reduce vulnerability, ease livelihoods, improve public services and generate sustainable economic returns.

The latest floods gave a painful signal that risk does not respect administrative boundaries, political promises or budget constraints. A bridge built without adequate consideration of flood risk, a settlement established in an unsafe corridor, can impose costs on generations of taxpayers. Thus, the challenge of development finance is about changing the investment incentives and institutions that shape public investment.

Political leaders should think beyond the volume of budget sanctioned for the physical structures that they will lay foundation stones for. The government must now stop the recurring cycle of construction, destruction and reconstruction by pursuing prudent public accountability and financial sustainability.

Public officials should dare to enforce scientific standards and to resist undue political pressure. Contractors must follow responsible business practices in compliance with quality and legal standards, whereas communities should be empowered to scrutinise the projects' dashboards and whittle down the violations. Most importantly, planners should dare to accept that disaster resilience is not an additional cost but rather a precondition for protecting development gains.





(The author is an applied economist with experience in economic policy and development research.)

title: All the Prime Minister’s Men - Nepali Times
description: All the Prime Minister’s Men  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
For Prime Minister Balendra Shah and his coterie of advisers, it has been an eventful week between the holidays, even as the rift between the RSP and its own government continues to grow.

The PMO has been dealing with several leaks involving national security and judicial institutions, ordering the detention of journalists (while denying it) who reported on the very same leaks, and holding bureaucrats at the PMO in order to prompt them into canceling an important irrigation project.

And it all climaxed with the dismissal of Inspector General of Police Dan Bahadur Karki on Wednesday. Is the government multi-tasking, or firefighting?

Spokesperson and Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel used doublespeak to explain that Karki was not technically ‘fired’ – he was simply ‘given a new responsibility’ of being the security adviser to the Prime Minister.

Manoj KC, who had long been PM Shah’s favoured pick to lead the police, is now Nepal’s top cop. He is the man responsible for investigating the fake refugee scandal two years ago that implicated those at the top levels of government.

There has been no love lost between the Prime Minister and Karki, who is said to have resisted the PM’s direct instructions to detain businessmen, political figures, and recently, former Chief Justice Cholendra Rana without due process.

But the straw that broke the camel’s back seems to have been the leaks over the last few days, including the government’s plan to replace Karki, and a correspondence between Supreme Court Justice Hari Phuyal and political fixer Inam Sapkota insinuating political interference in the judiciary.

Then, it emerged that Prime Minister’s adviser Kumar (Ben) Byanjankar had himself been in conversation with Sapkota, and had Sapkota’s personal phone in his possession for up to 48 hours before the police got it.

GROWING DIVIDE

These are surface ripples of a deeper undercurrent of distrust between Prime Minister Shah and the establishment faction of the governing RSP led by party chair Rabi Lamichhane. The PM makes impulsive decisions, and RSP lawmakers have to do damage control. At a recent RSP meeting some ministers are said to have complained that they learn of the PMO’s decisions through the media.

On the removal of the IGP at least, Shah is said to have conferred on the matter with Lamichhane, but went ahead with the sacking despite being told it was a bad idea.

Recent events have shown that the PMO has grown increasingly insular, with the Shah’s unelected advisers having unchecked authority to even deploy the intelligence and security apparatus to nab critics or scrap project tenders they do not like.

The latest example is senior officials from the Department of Irrigation were virtually kidnapped, and held by the police before being taken to the PMO for hostile interrogation and forced to rescind a tender bidding process for the much delayed Sunkosi Marin Diversion Project that would irrigate Tarai farms and generate 28MW of electricity.

That the PM’s advisers wield total authority over state institutions is not new information, it is out in the open and every incident proves it is happening. The Prime Minister himself has been posting snide comments that verge on threats, while his adviser is said to have a black list of 28 journalists critical of the government.

Ahead of a proposed visit to New Delhi later this month, PM Shah appears to have no intention of keeping his circle of advisers in check. But posting satirical quips on social media will only take Shah and his right hand men so far.

The RSP and Balendra Shah ran on a platform of cleaning up corruption and political collusion, promoting transparent government and holding the party leadership accountable. But the political and institutional rot that the PM promised to purge appears to have only burrowed deeper.

If the government is serious about setting itself apart from its predecessors, then the Prime Minister should treat the allegations over the motives and conduct of his adviser(s) with the same severity as he treats his opponents, his predecessors, businessmen, bankers, and other figures.

And the same public that elected Shah into office because of they trusted him to end institutionalised corruption, nepotism that has defined Nepali politics for at least the last two decades, should demand the same transparency and accountability of him and his team.

title: Parliamentary study identifies political divisions, weak commissions as obstacles to transitional justice in Nepal - OnlineKhabar English News
description: Parliamentary study identifies political divisions, weak commissions as obstacles to transitional justice in Nepal  OnlineKhabar English News
publisher.title: OnlineKhabar English News
full_article:
Kathmandu, November 6

Nearly two decades have passed since the Comprehensive Peace Accord formally ended Nepal’s armed conflict, but the transitional justice process remains unfinished.

A parliamentary subcommittee has now identified several obstacles to implementing the law governing transitional justice, ranging from a lack of political consensus to weak institutional autonomy and unmotivated staff at the commissions responsible for the process.

The Legislative Management Committee under the National Assembly had formed a subcommittee led by Dr Anjan Shakya to study and assess the implementation of selected laws.

Formed on July 20, the subcommittee selected six laws for review and submitted its report to the parent committee on October 30.

The laws include the Enforced Disappearances Enquiry, Truth and Reconciliation Commission Act, 2014, which governs the transitional justice process, as well as the Federation, Province and Local Level (Coordination and Interrelations) Act, 2020; the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority Act, 1991; the Electronic Transactions Act, 2006; the Legal Aid Act, 1997; and the Human Body Organ Transplantation (Regulation and Prohibition) Act, 1998.

The report includes an assessment of the implementation of the transitional justice law and an indicator-based analysis. It identifies five major problems.

First, transitional justice continues to be viewed primarily through the lens of conventional criminal justice. Second, the process requires political initiative and consensus, which remain inadequate. Third, victims have the right to appeal if they are dissatisfied with the commissions’ recommendations on reparation. Fourth, staff working in the commissions lack motivation. And fifth, the commissions do not appear to enjoy financial and administrative autonomy.

The Comprehensive Peace Accord was signed between the then government and the rebel Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) on November 21, 2006, formally ending the decade-long armed conflict. However, conflict victims have yet to receive full justice.

In its assessment, the subcommittee notes that a separate trust or fund has been established for transitional justice. The fund receives contributions from the international community, the Nepal government and other sources. However, it says political commitment and consistency are necessary to mobilise the fund to provide reparation and justice to conflict victims.

The report also recalls the background of the peace agreement and provisions of the Interim Constitution, noting that the transitional justice process did not advance as envisaged.

It states that the Enforced Disappearances Enquiry, Truth and Reconciliation Commission Act, 2014, was introduced following the Comprehensive Peace Accord to establish the truth and create conditions for reconciliation in society. The Act also provided the legal basis for establishing the commissions.

Yet the peace agreement, signed on November 21, 2006, had already stipulated that a Truth and Reconciliation Commission would be formed within six months.

Clause 5 of the agreement called for the formation of the commission within that period to investigate the truth about serious human rights violations and crimes against humanity committed during the conflict and promote reconciliation. Political disagreements and legal ambiguities, however, delayed the process for years.

While several other aspects of the peace process have been addressed, transitional justice remains unresolved.

The formal end of the decade-long conflict, the management of weapons held by Maoist combatants and their integration into the Nepal Army were among the major tasks completed under the peace process. But justice for conflict victims remains outstanding.

Against this backdrop, the parliamentary subcommittee has sought to identify why implementation of the transitional justice law has been delayed. Its findings point to the absence of political consensus, a lack of autonomy in the commissions and shortcomings in their institutional capacity and staffing.

The study says the approach to transitional justice remains constrained by the mindset that treats it solely as a conventional criminal justice process.

In other words, the problem lies partly in how transitional justice itself is understood.

Transitional justice is not simply a criminal justice procedure. It is intended to establish the truth about events during the conflict, provide justice and reparation to victims, and create an environment for reconciliation in society. Political commitment and consensus are equally important to achieving these objectives.

The subcommittee therefore stresses the need for a common understanding and consistent commitment among political parties. It says a shared political position is essential to move the process forward.

The report also identifies three broad challenges and possible measures for the coming days.

It notes a lack of political unity, commitment and priority in completing the remaining tasks of the peace process. It further says that the obstacles to implementing the law can be addressed only if the commissions are granted financial and administrative autonomy. At present, however, they lack such independence.

The subcommittee has also called for coordination and cooperation with donor countries and urged local, provincial and federal governments to focus on providing technical and administrative support and creating employment opportunities to protect and support victims.

The report highlights a lack of motivation among employees working in the commissions. It says the absence of institutional capacity and staff motivation has affected the work of bodies responsible for investigating, examining and establishing the truth about highly sensitive conflict-era cases.

The subcommittee concludes that providing the commissions with the independence, resources and administrative authority needed to function effectively would help advance the process of delivering justice to conflict victims, establishing the whereabouts of disappeared people and determining the truth about serious human rights violations.

The study also notes that victims can appeal against recommendations made by the commissions if they are dissatisfied. This provision is intended to ensure that the commissions’ recommendations are not treated as final without considering victims’ objections.

By emphasising victims’ participation and satisfaction, the report points to the importance of keeping avenues for judicial remedy open when the commissions’ recommendations fail to meet victims’ expectations of justice.

According to the parliamentary study, 17 regulations, directives and procedures have been introduced to support implementation of the Act.

The subcommittee examined these supporting legal and procedural instruments as part of its assessment. Although the legal and technical foundations for implementing the law have been established, effective implementation remains lacking. The report identifies political commitment, the commissions’ autonomy and the delivery of justice to victims as major challenges.

Khamm Khati, a member of the parliamentary subcommittee, says the central purpose of transitional justice goes beyond documenting conflict-era incidents and investigating complaints.

Its core objectives are to ensure that victims receive justice and reparation, establish the truth and create lasting conditions for reconciliation in society.

“Along with making laws and procedures, the task now is to ensure political consensus, strengthen the institutional capacity of the commissions and guarantee justice for victims,” he said. “But once again, the government does not appear to have given this issue priority.”

Khati said the law minister had expressed a commitment to implementing provisions related to the transitional justice law, but the government’s actions had not reflected that commitment.

“The commissions are without office-bearers. Work needs to begin there first,” he said. “The commissions need to be formed, and the complaints they have received need to be examined and taken forward.”

On May 5, 2026, the government issued the Special Ordinance on the Removal of Public Office-holders, 2026. Under the ordinance, the then office-bearers of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the Commission of Investigation on Enforced Disappeared Persons were removed from their positions.

The vacant positions have not been filled since then.

With the office-bearers removed through the ordinance and no new appointments made, the commissions have been unable to carry out their work.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission initially received 63,718 complaints. However, following amendments to the Act in 2024, the deadline for filing complaints was extended, particularly to allow conflict victims who had previously been unable to register complaints to come forward. These included women who had suffered sexual violence and rape during the conflict.

More than 15,000 additional complaints were registered during the extended period. The commission now has a total of 78,909 complaints.

publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
After an Indian official said in October 2026 there had been standoffs between Indian and Chinese troops at the Himalayan frontier of Arunachal Pradesh, a video circulated online with the false claim it showed Indian villagers chasing away Chinese soldiers. AFP geolocated the clip to a village in western Nepal, while a local official said it depicts a religious festival.

"Villagers in Arunachal clashed with the Chinese army," reads a Hindi-language Facebook post uploaded on October 28.

The attached footage shows a crowd running through a hillside agricultural area. Text superimposed on it reads: "Villagers chased away the Chinese army in Arunachal".

Screenshot of false Facebook post taken November 5, 2026, with red X added by AFP

The post surfaced after a top Indian border police official Shatrujeet Kapur reported "face offs" between Indian and Chinese forces at multiple locations along the border in Arunachal Pradesh ( archived link).

China claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of southern Tibet, while India says the state is an integral part of its territory. Tens of thousands of troops patrol the area.

India's foreign ministry following Kapur's comments said the two sides remained in regular contact to manage border tensions ( archived link).

China also responded by saying its troops were carrying out routine patrols and border management activities, and that Beijing had consistently followed agreements and understandings reached between the neighbouring Asian giants ( archived link).

The video was also shared online with similar claims in Myanmar, which shares borders with Arunachal Pradesh.

Myanmar is not a party to the dispute, but China has been the junta's most crucial ally and a rare enduring partner after Min Aung Hlaing's 2021 coup ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, which triggered a war with armed groups supporting the civilian government ( archived link).

However, the circulating video was filmed in Nepal and is not linked to the China-India border tensions.

Dashain festival

A reverse image search on Google using keyframes from the falsely shared video led to a higher-quality version uploaded on Facebook on October 26 with the caption "Woyl" ( archived link).

Screenshot comparison of falsely shared video (L) and original clip

Further reverse image and keyword searches surfaced another video of the same event from a different angle, captioned "Wayal Purnima Fair 2k83" ( archived link).

Wayal, also known as Woyl, is a village located in the Doti district of Nepal's western Sudurpashchim province ( archived link).

The Office of Rural Municipal Executive in Doti told AFP in an email on November 4: "The activities shown in the video are related to local traditional and cultural practices during the Dashain festival" ( archived link).

Dashain is the longest annual two-week Hindu festival, honouring the Universal Mother Goddess Durga (archived here and here).

During the festival, people from other urban centres return to their ancestral villages for family gatherings.

A local journalist in Nepal separately said the video depicts a buffalo sacrifice performed during the Dashain festival. He provided AFP with another Facebook video from the area showing the event ( archived link).

The footage matches Google Street View imagery of Wayal village, more than 1,000 kilometres (620 miles) away from Arunachal Pradesh ( archived link).

Screenshot comparison of original video (L) and Google Street View imagery of Wayal village, with corresponding elements highlighted by AFP

AFP has previously debunked other false claims stemming from tensions along the India-China border.

title: California Sherpa Association transfers NPR 17 million to Nepal’s relief fund - The Tourism Times
description: California Sherpa Association transfers NPR 17 million to Nepal’s relief fund  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: The California Sherpa Association has transferred more than 17 million rupees to Nepal’s Prime Minister Disaster Relief Fund to support communities affected by recent floods in the country.



Gombu Sherpa, president of the CSA, said that, on behalf of the association, he had transferred USD 116,046.66 to the PMDRF’s Himalayan Bank account on November 2.



“The fund, amounting to over NPR 17 million, has been directly channelled to the PMDRF account as per the decision of the association,” Sherpa said.



The California Sherpa Association, along with the Himalayan Sherpa Club of Sonoma, organised a fundraising event last month, according to Sherpa.





During “Sonoma for Nepal: A Flood Relief Charity Dinner,” held at the Sonoma Veterans Memorial Hall with support from the City of Sonoma, the organisers collected the amount from the Nepali community and other donors.



Hundreds of community members and dignitaries attended the event, with restaurants, wineries, and volunteer organisations also joining the humanitarian initiative. Members of the Sherpa community offered Buddhist prayers for those who lost their lives in the floods.



A video showing the devastation caused by the August 26 floods along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli corridors was also screened during the programme. People from different parts of the San Francisco Bay Area attended the event in solidarity with Nepal.



Sonoma Mayor Ron Wellander and Representative Mike Thompson of California’s 4th Congressional District also attended the event and praised the Sherpa community’s efforts to support flood-affected communities in Nepal, according to Sherpa.





The event not only raised relief funds but also united the Nepali diaspora for a good cause, said Pemba Sherpa, president of the Himalayan Sherpa Club of Sonoma. “It reflected the continuing connection between the Nepali diaspora and their homeland, as our bond with Nepal is getting stronger even though we live miles away from the homeland,” he said.



The association also extended heartfelt thanks to all the wineries and restaurants that generously donated their time, food, and wine. “We are also immensely grateful to all our donors, whether you gave online, mailed in your contributions, or joined us in person,” it said. “We thank the City of Sonoma, the City Council, and Sonoma County for their support and partnership.”
